title: The DA Delay Tax: What a Slow Planning Approval Really Costs a Property Developer
excerpt: World Town Planning Day falls this week. For property developers the real cost of a slow DA approval isn't the wait itself, it's everything that keeps accruing quietly underneath it.
content:
World Town Planning Day lands this week, which is a fitting moment to say something most property developers already feel in their bones: a council's assessment timeline is not a scheduling detail, it is a financial variable with a dollar value attached.

A development that sits with council for an extra four or five months doesn't just push the start date out. Every cost that was supposed to be funded by an early construction start keeps accruing anyway. Land holding costs, consultant retainers, interest on acquisition finance, rates, none of it pauses because the development application hasn't been issued.

The number that eventually decides whether the project still works isn't the feasibility study signed off at acquisition. It's the one that gets quietly redone, usually under pressure, once the planning timeline blows out and the presale and finance clock keeps ticking regardless.

The presale clock doesn't wait for the DA clock

Most construction finance facilities are conditional on a presale threshold, commonly somewhere between 60 and 70 percent of a project's end value sold before the bank will release funds to build. Buyers sign off-the-plan contracts well ahead of construction, and those contracts carry a sunset clause, a date by which settlement must occur or the buyer can walk away and have their deposit returned. A DA delay doesn't just cost time. It eats directly into the gap between the day presales were locked in and the day the sunset clause expires, the exact window the finance approval is supposed to fit inside.

The pattern we typically see is that developers model the DA timeline on the planning consultant's best case, because that's what the letter says, and the finance is structured around that date. When council runs long, and across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria it regularly does, the sunset clock and the finance clock stop lining up. Buyers who signed twelve months earlier at one price are now settling into a market that may have moved against them, and some don't settle at all.

Capitalised interest doesn't feel like a cost until it is one

Interest on land acquisition and holding finance during the approval period is usually capitalised, added to the loan balance rather than paid in cash each month. That structure makes sense while the project is waiting on approval, because there's no income yet to service debt from. It also means the cost of the delay doesn't show up anywhere obvious while it's happening. No invoice lands, no cash leaves the account, the loan balance simply grows a little further every month the DA sits with council.

The reckoning arrives at completion, when the capitalised interest is repaid out of sale proceeds alongside everything else. A development that looked like a comfortable margin at acquisition can land well below that once an extended holding period and the consultant fees that came with it are actually totalled up. The project didn't get any less good. The holding period got longer, and that cost didn't disappear just because nobody paid it in real time. A banking and facility review run before a facility is drawn down, rather than after a delay has already happened, is the point where this kind of exposure is still something a developer can negotiate, not just absorb.

Price the council timeline like the variable it actually is

Feasibility studies built on a single DA date are feasibility studies built on hope. A more useful version runs the same project through three timelines, on schedule, three months over, and six months over, and shows where the margin actually breaks. For a lot of projects, there's a council delay somewhere in the second or third scenario that turns a comfortable return into a project that barely covers its own holding costs. Developers who build this kind of cash flow discipline into the feasibility stage, rather than only once construction is underway, tend to spot a tightening project well before it becomes an urgent one.

None of this is a reason to avoid development. It's a reason to treat the planning timeline as a line item with a dollar value, the same way a quantity surveyor treats a construction cost blowout. A fractional CFO partner working alongside a development through acquisition, DA and construction can keep the feasibility model honest as the timeline actually unfolds, rather than finding out at settlement that the margin moved months earlier. If a project on your books is sitting longer with council than the feasibility assumed, book a discovery call and bring the current feasibility with you.

faqs.q: How does a DA delay actually affect a property development's finance?
faqs.a: A delayed development application keeps every holding cost running, land finance interest, consultant retainers, rates, while pushing the construction start date out. Because presales carry sunset clauses and construction finance usually needs a presale threshold met, a longer approval period can put both the buyer contracts and the funding timeline at risk at the same time, not just the build schedule.

faqs.q: What presale percentage do banks typically require before releasing construction finance?
faqs.a: It varies by lender and project, but a presale threshold somewhere between 60 and 70 percent of end value is common before a bank will fund construction. The important detail isn't the exact number, it's whether the sunset clauses on those presale contracts still have enough runway left once the actual DA timeline, rather than the planned one, becomes clear.

faqs.q: Why is capitalised interest considered a hidden cost in property development?
faqs.a: Capitalised interest is added to the loan balance rather than paid in cash during the holding period, so it never appears as a monthly expense while the project waits on approval. It only becomes visible at completion, when it's repaid out of sale proceeds alongside everything else, often making the realised margin noticeably thinner than the acquisition feasibility assumed.

faqs.q: Should a property developer model more than one planning approval timeline?
faqs.a: Yes. A feasibility study built around a single best case DA date tends to understate risk. Running the same project through an on schedule scenario and two delayed scenarios shows where the margin actually breaks, which is a more useful input into cash flow planning than a single optimistic number carried through to settlement.

faqs.q: What happens if a buyer's sunset clause expires before settlement occurs?
faqs.a: If settlement hasn't happened by the sunset date, the buyer generally has the right to terminate the contract and have their deposit returned. For the developer, that can mean losing part of the presale coverage a construction facility was approved against, right at the point the project needs that funding certainty the most.

faqs.q: Does council approval timing vary much across Queensland, NSW and Victoria?
faqs.a: Timelines differ between councils and states, and within a single council from one year to the next depending on workload and the complexity of a given application. The practical implication is the same everywhere on the east coast, a feasibility study anchored to one assumed DA date is a feasibility study exposed to a variable the developer doesn't control.

faqs.q: When should a property developer bring in a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: Earlier than most expect, ideally around acquisition, so the feasibility model, facility terms and presale strategy are built together rather than reconciled after a delay has already happened. A fractional CFO partnership keeps the commercial model current as the actual DA and construction timeline unfolds, not just at the two points the bank asks for an update.
